data.text:
🙏🇺🇸🙏

It is April 19, 1967. North Vietnam. Major Leo Thorsness sits in the cockpit of an F-105F Wild Weasel. He is flying at 600 miles per hour.
His job is to bait anti-aircraft batteries. He forces the surface-to-air missile sites to turn on their radar. When they lock onto him, he fires back. His Electronic Warfare Officer, Harold Johnson, sits in the rear seat, staring at the scopes. They have logged 92 missions. The Air Force considers 100 missions a full combat tour. The math says they are almost done.
The radio cracks open. It is their wingman. His plane took a direct hit.
Thorsness watches the trailing F-105 burst into a tight bloom of orange fire. Two parachutes deploy.
Safety protocol dictates a return to base when a flight lead loses his wingman. Thorsness pushes the stick forward instead. He drops his nose toward the descending parachutes. He circles the airspace. He needs to keep the rescue helicopters updated on the drift.

At the time, Seventh Air Force tactical doctrine did not require a Wild Weasel to loiter over a hostile crash site. Standard operating procedure prioritized the preservation of the specialized electronic warfare aircraft. The 1966 tactical manuals explicitly warned against low-speed orbits in heavy anti-aircraft artillery zones.
Thorsness was flying in direct violation of the math.
A Soviet-built MiG-17 drops from the cloud cover.
Thorsness turns his bulky fighter toward the lighter, faster interceptor. It is a terrible mismatch.
The G-forces push the blood into his boots. His vision narrows to a tunnel. He fires a burst from his 20mm cannon. The MiG breaks away.
Then another MiG appears. Then three more.
He flies in a tight circle around the parachutes.
The fuel gauge drops near zero. He leaves the airspace to find a KC-135 tanker over Laos. He takes just enough fuel to get back to the fight. He returns to the crash site. He shoots down another mig.
A rescue helicopter is finally approaching. But another American pilot comes over the radio. He is out of gas. If he doesn't hit the tanker immediately, he will drop into the jungle.
On April 30, a heat-seeking missile shreds the back of his F-105. He ejects at 600 miles per hour.
The wind tears his legs apart. He hits the dirt with shattered knees.

His flight boots are gone. They were ripped off his feet in the slipstream. He is dragged three miles through the brush in his socks. One of his captors wears a silver watch stolen from an American pilot the week before.
They put him in Hoa Lo Prison. They call it the Hanoi Hilton.
The interrogation lasts eighteen days. He does not sleep. They bend his ruined legs until he passes out. He wakes up and they do it again.
He learns to tap on the concrete walls. The prisoners use a code. The seasons change outside. He tracks them by the temperature of the floor. He hears tapping from the cell next door. It is another pilot with a crushed shoulder.
Thorsness has a bowl of pumpkin water and a half-ration of rice.
He limps to the shared wall. He finds a crack near the floorboards. He pushes half his rice through the hole.
On March 4, 1973, a C-141 Starlifter lands at Clark Air Base in the Philippines. Thorsness walks down the ramp. He walks slowly. His legs are stiff. The silence on the tarmac is heavy. Nobody is shooting. Nobody is tapping on a wall.

He is 41 years old. He looks 60.
The military drew up the paperwork for the Medal of Honor in 1967. They locked it in a safe. They did not want his captors to know they were holding him. President Nixon puts the medal around his neck in October 1973. Thorsness retires as a colonel.
He moves to Washington State. He serves in the state senate. The F-105 he flew is scrapped for metal in the 1980s. The prison in Hanoi is largely demolished in 1993. It is turned into a commercial complex with a small museum. The wall where he tapped the code is gone. He dies in 2017. The citation for his medal sits in the National Archives, filed under Record Group 330 🙏🇺🇸🙏

quoted_tweet.text:
🙏🇺🇸🙏

Before war, Jessica Ellis spent her summers fighting wildfires in the Fremont Winema National Forest. Smoke, exhaustion, heat, and long nights taught her something early. When people are in danger, someone has to step forward.
After college, she chose the Army. She trained as a combat medic because helping others was not an abstract idea to her. It was a responsibility.
Assigned to the 101st Airborne Division, she deployed to Iraq in late 2005, working in base clinics and riding out with combat engineers on dangerous clearance missions through Baghdad.
She faced explosions more than once and kept going.

In 2007, she returned to Baghdad for another deployment. In April 2008, an explosive device struck her vehicle. She survived. Many would have taken that as a warning. Jessica did not.
On May 11, 2008, another medic could not go out on patrol. Jessica volunteered to take her place. She refused to let her teammates move without medical support.
That decision cost her life.
Her vehicle was attacked and set on fire. Her teammates dragged her free and fought to save her, refusing to give up on the person who had never given up on them. She was only 24.
When her father spoke to her unit, they did not talk about medals first. They talked about her spirit. They said she kept morale high. They said she was always there.
Jessica Ellis was posthumously promoted to corporal and awarded the Bronze Star and Purple Heart. She now rests at Arlington National Cemetery.
Some courage does not shout. It simply shows up, even when it knows the risk 🙏🇺🇸🙏

ONE OF THE WORST NIGHTCLUB FIRES

#OnThisDay in 1996, a fire broke out in Ozone Disco in Quezon City, killing 162 people, mostly youth, while 95 others were hurt in the tragedy.

The numerous deaths were attributed to the lack of fire safety measures inside the building, as well as the improper installation of the exit door which swung inward rather than outward.
